title.en: Section 1 - A conversation about arranging a birthday party
title.zh: 第一部分 - 关于安排生日派对的对话

sections.passage: A conversation between a customer, Karen, and a party organiser, Paul, about arranging a surprise birthday party for Karen's husband. Karen calls the Event Centre to book a venue and discuss the arrangements. She wants to hold the party on Saturday, November 15th, for approximately 40 guests. Paul explains that they have two main function rooms available: the Garden Room, which holds up to 30 people, and the Grand Hall, which can accommodate up to 80 people. Since Karen expects around 40 guests, the Grand Hall would be more suitable. The hire cost for the Grand Hall is 350 pounds for the evening, which includes basic decorations, tables, and chairs. Karen asks about catering options. Paul explains that they work with three local catering companies and can offer buffet-style meals starting at 18 pounds per person, which includes a selection of hot and cold dishes, or a sit-down three-course dinner at 30 pounds per person. Karen decides on the buffet option to keep costs down. Paul mentions that they also offer a DJ service for 200 pounds and a photographer for 150 pounds for three hours. Karen is interested in the DJ but not the photographer, as her sister will take photos. Paul says they can arrange a special birthday cake through a local bakery for an additional 45 pounds. Karen provides her contact details and asks Paul to send her a written quotation by email. She pays a non-refundable deposit of 100 pounds to secure the booking.

title.en: Section 2 - A talk about a wildlife conservation project
title.zh: 第二部分 - 关于野生动物保护项目的介绍

sections.passage: A presentation by Dr. Laura Chen about a wildlife conservation project in the Scottish Highlands. The project, called Highland Rewilding, was established five years ago with the aim of restoring native habitats and reintroducing species that had been driven to extinction in the region. Dr. Chen explains that the project covers an area of approximately 10,000 hectares of land, which was formerly used for sheep farming and deer stalking. The first phase of the project focused on planting native trees, particularly Scots pine, birch, and rowan. Over the past five years, volunteers have planted more than 500,000 trees across the site. The second phase involved the reintroduction of the Eurasian beaver, which had been absent from Scotland for over 400 years. Twenty beavers were initially released, and the population has since grown to approximately 65 individuals. Dr. Chen explains that beavers are considered a keystone species because their dam-building activities create wetland habitats that benefit many other species, including otters, water voles, and various bird species. The project's third phase, which is currently underway, focuses on the reintroduction of wildcats, one of Britain's most endangered mammals. Dr. Chen notes that fewer than 300 pure wildcats remain in the wild, making conservation efforts critical. The project has faced some opposition from local farmers concerned about crop damage and livestock predation, but the team has worked closely with the farming community to address these concerns through compensation schemes and fencing solutions. The project also operates an education programme, hosting school visits and community workshops to raise awareness about biodiversity and conservation.

title.en: Section 3 - Two students discussing a presentation on renewable energy
title.zh: 第三部分 - 两名学生讨论关于可再生能源的演讲

sections.passage: A conversation between two postgraduate students, Tom and Priya, who are preparing a joint presentation on renewable energy sources for their Environmental Engineering seminar. They have been asked to compare three types of renewable energy: solar, wind, and hydroelectric power. Tom has been researching solar energy and has found that the cost of solar panels has decreased by approximately 89 percent over the past decade, making it one of the cheapest forms of new electricity generation in many parts of the world. He mentions that the largest solar farm in the world, the Bhadla Solar Park in India, has a capacity of 2,245 megawatts and covers an area of 14,000 acres. However, Tom points out that solar energy has the limitation of intermittency, meaning it can only generate electricity when the sun is shining. Priya has been focusing on wind energy. She explains that modern wind turbines can generate up to 12 megawatts of power each, and that the global wind energy capacity exceeded 800 gigawatts by the end of 2022. She highlights that offshore wind farms are becoming increasingly important because winds at sea tend to be stronger and more consistent than on land. The Hornsea Wind Farm off the coast of Yorkshire is currently the largest in the world, with a capacity of 2.8 gigawatts. They discuss hydroelectric power together and agree that while it provides reliable, consistent energy and accounts for approximately 16 percent of global electricity production, it has significant environmental impacts, including the displacement of communities and disruption of river ecosystems. They decide to present their findings using a comparative framework that evaluates each energy source in terms of cost, reliability, environmental impact, and scalability. Tom suggests they include a case study of Denmark, which generates over 50 percent of its electricity from wind power.

title.en: Section 4 - A lecture on the history of cartography
title.zh: 第四部分 - 关于制图学历史的讲座

sections.passage: A university lecture by Professor David Armstrong on the history of cartography, the science and art of map-making. Professor Armstrong begins by explaining that the earliest known maps date back to ancient Babylon, around 2300 BC, where maps were drawn on clay tablets. The Babylonians depicted their world as a flat disc surrounded by water, with Babylon at the centre. The ancient Greeks made significant advances in cartography. Eratosthenes, who lived in the third century BC, calculated the circumference of the Earth with remarkable accuracy by measuring the angle of the sun's shadow at two different locations in Egypt. His estimate of approximately 40,000 kilometres was remarkably close to the modern measurement of 40,075 kilometres. Ptolemy, a Greek-Roman scholar writing in the second century AD, created a comprehensive guide to geography that included coordinates for approximately 8,000 locations. His work remained influential for over a thousand years. During the medieval period in Europe, map-making was dominated by religious perspectives. The most common type of map was the mappa mundi, which placed Jerusalem at the centre of the world and emphasised biblical events and locations rather than geographical accuracy. The most famous surviving example is the Hereford Mappa Mundi, created around 1300, which is displayed in Hereford Cathedral in England. The Age of Exploration in the 15th and 16th centuries revolutionised cartography. The development of the magnetic compass, the astrolabe, and later the sextant enabled navigators to determine their position at sea with increasing accuracy. Gerardus Mercator's world map of 1569, which used a cylindrical projection that allowed sailors to plot straight-line courses, became the standard for nautical navigation and remains the basis for most world maps used today. The lecture concludes by discussing modern cartography, including satellite-based Global Positioning Systems and digital mapping technologies that have transformed how we create and use maps.

title.en: Passage 1 - The Development of the Bicycle
title.zh: 文章1 - 自行车的发展

sections.passage: The bicycle is one of the most efficient and widely used forms of transportation in human history, yet its development spans nearly two centuries of innovation, experimentation, and refinement. The earliest precursor to the modern bicycle was the 'running machine' or 'draisine', invented by the German Baron Karl von Drais in 1817. This device had two wheels in line, connected by a wooden frame, and was propelled by the rider pushing their feet against the ground. It had no pedals, brakes, or chain drive, and was made almost entirely of wood. Despite its limitations, the draisine created considerable excitement in Europe and America, though it was soon banned from sidewalks in many cities due to the danger it posed to pedestrians. The next major breakthrough came in the 1860s, when Pierre Michaux, a French blacksmith, is credited with attaching pedals directly to the front wheel of a velocipede, creating the first true pedal-driven bicycle. These early pedal bicycles, sometimes called 'boneshakers' because of their uncomfortable ride on iron-rimmed wheels and rough roads, became hugely popular despite their drawbacks. The high bicycle, or penny-farthing, appeared in the 1870s and featured a very large front wheel and a much smaller rear wheel. The large front wheel allowed for greater speed with each pedal rotation, but the high seating position made it extremely dangerous, as riders could easily be thrown over the handlebars. The modern safety bicycle, which closely resembles the bicycles we ride today, was developed in the 1880s. John Kemp Starley's Rover safety bicycle, produced in 1885, featured two wheels of equal size, a chain-driven rear wheel, and a diamond-shaped frame. This design was far more stable and accessible than its predecessors, and it quickly made the penny-farthing obsolete. The pneumatic tyre, invented by John Boyd Dunlop in 1888, further improved comfort and performance. By the 1890s, the bicycle had become a symbol of personal freedom and independence, particularly for women, who found that cycling gave them unprecedented mobility and contributed to the growing movement for social reform.

title.en: Passage 2 - The Impact of Noise Pollution on Health
title.zh: 文章2 - 噪音污染对健康的影响

sections.passage: Noise pollution is an increasingly serious environmental problem that affects millions of people worldwide, yet it receives far less attention than air or water pollution. The World Health Organisation has described noise pollution as a modern plague, estimating that in Europe alone, long-term exposure to environmental noise causes approximately 12,000 premature deaths and 48,000 new cases of ischaemic heart disease every year. Sound is measured in decibels, and prolonged exposure to noise levels above 85 decibels can cause permanent hearing damage. For reference, normal conversation typically registers at around 60 decibels, heavy traffic at 85 decibels, a rock concert at 110 decibels, and a jet engine at close range at 140 decibels. Research has consistently shown that chronic exposure to noise pollution has wide-ranging health effects beyond hearing loss. A major study conducted by the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine found that for every 10-decibel increase in nighttime noise levels, the risk of cardiovascular events increased by 14 percent. This is because noise triggers the body's stress response, releasing hormones such as cortisol and adrenaline, which raise blood pressure and heart rate. Over time, this chronic stress response can lead to hypertension, heart disease, and stroke. Noise pollution also has significant effects on mental health and cognitive performance. Studies have shown that children who attend schools near airports or busy roads perform worse on standardised reading tests and have difficulty concentrating. A landmark study in Germany found that children living near Cologne airport showed measurable improvements in reading comprehension and long-term memory after the airport relocated. In adults, chronic noise exposure has been linked to increased rates of anxiety, depression, and sleep disturbance. Addressing noise pollution requires a multi-faceted approach, including urban planning that separates residential areas from noise sources, the development of quieter transportation technologies, better sound insulation in buildings, and the creation of quiet zones in urban areas where people can escape the constant bombardment of noise.

title.en: Passage 3 - The Future of Food Production
title.zh: 文章3 - 食品生产的未来

sections.passage: As the global population approaches 10 billion by 2050, the challenge of feeding humanity sustainably has become one of the most pressing issues of our time. Current food production systems are already under enormous strain, with agriculture responsible for approximately 25 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, 70 percent of freshwater withdrawals, and significant deforestation and biodiversity loss. Finding ways to produce more food with fewer environmental impacts will require fundamental changes in how we grow, process, and consume food. One promising approach is vertical farming, which involves growing crops in stacked layers within controlled indoor environments. Vertical farms can produce up to 350 times more food per square metre than conventional agriculture, while using up to 95 percent less water through recirculating irrigation systems. Because the growing environment is fully controlled, vertical farms can operate year-round regardless of weather conditions and do not require pesticides or herbicides. Companies such as AeroFarms in the United States and Infarm in Germany have built large-scale vertical farms that supply fresh produce to major supermarket chains. However, vertical farming currently remains limited to leafy greens and herbs, as the energy costs of growing calorie-dense crops such as wheat and rice indoors remain prohibitively high. Another revolutionary development is cellular agriculture, which involves producing animal products such as meat, milk, and eggs from cell cultures rather than from whole animals. In 2013, the first laboratory-grown burger was produced at Maastricht University in the Netherlands at a cost of approximately 250,000 pounds. By 2023, the cost of cultivated meat had fallen to approximately 10 dollars per pound, and several companies have received regulatory approval to sell cultivated chicken and beef in certain markets. Proponents argue that cultivated meat could reduce greenhouse gas emissions associated with meat production by up to 92 percent while using 95 percent less land and 78 percent less water. Precision agriculture, which uses technologies such as GPS, drones, artificial intelligence, and satellite imagery to optimise farming practices, represents another important avenue for improving food production efficiency. These technologies allow farmers to apply fertilisers, pesticides, and water precisely where and when they are needed, reducing waste and environmental impact while increasing yields.
